aliases.name: Bathtub of Ice
aliases.meaning: from the central image of the legend

description.summary: A widely circulated late-20th-century urban legend in which a traveler, often male, is drugged by a stranger and wakes in a bathtub of ice with a fresh surgical incision and a note instructing them to call 911 because their kidney has been removed for the black market.
description.full: The 'kidney thieves' or 'kidney heist' urban legend is one of the most heavily documented modern American urban legends. In its canonical form a businessman or traveler meets an attractive stranger at a bar (most commonly in New Orleans, Las Vegas, or another convention city), accepts a drink, blacks out, and awakens hours later in a hotel bathtub filled with ice; a phone is placed beside the tub and a note instructs them to call 911 immediately, where they are told that one or both of their kidneys have been surgically removed and almost certainly sold on the black market. The legend was tracked from at least 1991 by folklorists and journalists, and from the mid-1990s by Snopes, the National Kidney Foundation, and law-enforcement agencies. It spread explosively as one of the first major chain-email legends in 1996–97. Despite intense investigation by police, transplant medicine professionals, and journalists, no documented case matching the legend has ever been substantiated; it is now a textbook example in folklore studies of an organ-theft 'contemporary legend' (Jan Harold Brunvand). It is distinct from the real, separately documented problem of organ trafficking (e.g., the 2008 Gurgaon kidney scandal in India), which involves consenting-but-coerced or deceived donors, not surreptitious surgical kidnapping.

etymology.origin: Folkloric coinage; the phrase 'Kidney Heist' is journalistic.
etymology.meaning: Self-explanatory: legend about kidneys being stolen.
etymology.first_use: Folklore tracking dates the canonical 'bathtub of ice' form to 1991; the version went viral on email circa 1996–1997.

patterns: Spreads through retelling and chain media
Localizes to whichever city the teller wants to warn against
Recurs predictably with each new communication medium (email in the 1990s, Facebook in the 2000s, TikTok in the 2010s–20s)

range.description: Originated in the United States and spread worldwide via email and social media; localized variants exist in many countries.
regions: United States (esp. New Orleans, Las Vegas, New York)

hotspots.name: New Orleans, Louisiana

location.description: Recurring fictional setting in early American versions of the legend

hotspots.notes: Hotel bars in New Orleans were so often named in the legend that the New Orleans Police Department issued public statements denying any such cases.

hotspots.name: Las Vegas, Nevada

location.description: Frequent setting for the chain-email variant

hotspots.notes: Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department also publicly debunked the rumor.

first_recorded.source: Snopes; Jan Harold Brunvand's contemporary-legend tracking

peak_activity_periods.description: Email-forward era; National Kidney Foundation issues formal denials
Plot device adopted in TV (e.g., Law & Order) and film, sustaining recognition
Recurs on Facebook and TikTok in localized warning posts

origins.cultural_roots: Late-20th-century anxieties about travel, strangers, organ-transplant medicine, and bodily commodification; structurally related to older 'body harvesting' rumors.
origins.earliest_accounts: Folklore tracking by Snopes and Jan Harold Brunvand places the canonical American form to 1991; antecedent rumors of organ theft circulated in Central and South America in the late 1980s.
origins.folklore_connections: Part of the modern American 'urban legend' canon (Brunvand) and the broader 'organ-theft' rumor cluster studied by Véronique Campion-Vincent and others.

timeline.event: Rumors of child organ theft spread in Central and South America, drawing condemnation from the U.S. Information Agency
Earliest documented American-style bathtub-of-ice tellings of the kidney-theft legend tracked by folklorists
The legend goes viral as an early major email forward, often citing fictional New Orleans police bulletins
timeline.significance: First mass-viral spread on the internet
timeline.source: Snopes; New Orleans Police Department public statement (1997)

timeline.event: Spokesman-Review and other regional U.S. newspapers cover the rumor, quoting officials calling it an 'urban myth run amok'
Véronique Campion-Vincent publishes 'Organ Theft Narratives' in the Western Folklore journal
timeline.significance: Academic anchoring of the legend within folkloristics

timeline.event: National Kidney Foundation issues a formal statement asking any actual victim to come forward; none does
The Gurgaon kidney scandal is exposed in India — a real organ-trafficking ring exploiting impoverished donors, structurally distinct from the legend
timeline.significance: Often cited in coverage of the legend; underscores that real organ trafficking exists but does not match the bathtub-of-ice scenario
timeline.source: Times of India and international coverage

history.modern_era: The legend has been thoroughly debunked by Snopes, law enforcement, transplant medicine specialists, and folklorists, but recurs reliably on each new social-media platform. It is widely taught in folklore-studies courses as a key example of contemporary legend dynamics.

documentary.name: Snopes — 'Kidney Theft' (1996, updated)
documentary.description: Long-running fact-check tracking the legend's history and variants; rates it 'False'.

documentary.name: National Kidney Foundation public statement
documentary.description: Statement asking any actual victim of involuntary kidney theft to come forward; none has been confirmed.

documentary.name: Campion-Vincent — 'Organ Theft Narratives' (1997)
documentary.description: Foundational folklore-studies analysis of the international organ-theft legend complex.

scientific.name: Medical impossibility
scientific.description: Transplant surgeons and nephrologists note the legend is not medically plausible: kidney harvesting requires HLA matching, sterile operative conditions, and cold-chain logistics far beyond what a hotel room could supply, and no organ is wasted in the manner the legend implies.
evidence_cited: Specialized surgical staffing and equipment needs

skeptical.name: Contemporary legend (folkloristic)
skeptical.description: The bathtub-of-ice story is a contemporary legend whose endurance is sociological: it encodes anxieties about travel, sexual strangers, and the medical commodification of the body.
evidence_cited: No verified case in over three decades of investigation
Repeating, mutating narrative pattern across regions
Rapid spread on each new communications platform

stories: The hotel-bar drink and the bathtub of ice
folklore.beliefs: Beware accepting drinks from strangers in unfamiliar cities; the human body can be reduced to a market commodity.

literature: Jan Harold Brunvand — The Baby Train and Other Lusty Urban Legends (1993, follow-ups in later collections)

Law & Order franchise — multiple plotlines invoking the legend
other: Frequent appearance in stand-up comedy and 'bad date' jokes
Recurring meme template on Facebook and TikTok
Cited in airline and hotel industry security-awareness training as a 'do not believe this' example
